feature: A file the canvas cannot place says no while you drag it
summary: Dragging a text file, an archive, a folder or any other non-picture over the canvas now shows the no-entry pointer from the moment it is over the picture, instead of the copy pointer followed by nothing happening. Pictures and Photonz documents are taken exactly as before.
setup: Photonz Dev, release Next. Nothing to turn on: this is how the canvas answers every drag.

try.do: Open any picture, or press Command N for a blank canvas.
Drag a .txt file from the Finder over the middle of the canvas and hold it there.
Watch the pointer: it should show the no-entry sign, and the canvas should draw no landing box.
Let go. Nothing lands, and the file springs back to the Finder.
Now drag a PNG over the same spot and hold it.
Watch the pointer show the copy badge and the canvas outline the box the picture would fill, then let go and see it land there.
Drag a folder over the canvas: it reads as refused too.

evaluate: Does the refusal read as the app being clear rather than the app being broken?
Is the no-entry pointer enough on its own, or did you want the app to say why the file cannot go there?
Did any file you would expect to land get refused?
Does a picture dragged straight after a refused file still feel instant?
rough: A screen capture cannot include the pointer, so the shots show what the canvas draws (a landing box for a picture, nothing for a text file) rather than the pointer glyph itself. The refusal is what the canvas answers the drag with, which is what makes macOS draw the no-entry sign.

Only the canvas refuses. Drop the same text file on the right hand panel or the chrome around the picture and the window still takes it and does nothing, because a window wide drop target sits behind the canvas. Filed as its own task.
A file is judged by its header, not its name: a .png full of text is refused, and a picture too corrupt to read its size is refused rather than accepted and then dropped on the floor.
A .photonz document is still accepted over the canvas even though it opens a window rather than landing, which is right, but it means the pointer promises a copy for something that is really an open.
